families.name: Knowledge Graph Embeddings
families.definition: Methods that represent entities and relationships in knowledge graphs as low-dimensional continuous vectors to perform tasks like link prediction.

properties.text: These methods use geometric translations or complex space rotations to model relation patterns such as symmetry, antisymmetry, and composition.
They achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in knowledge base completion and link prediction tasks.
Embedding models can be evaluated using unified frameworks to assess reproducibility and performance across different implementations.
Some variants, like CrossE, simulate crossover interactions between entities and relations to generate triple-specific embeddings.
Multi-view clustering frameworks can be used to overcome the weak-semantic nature of standard geometric translation score functions.

limitations.text: Embedding models are often black-box systems that lack interpretability and human-understandable insights.
They suffer from data sparsity and cold-start problems in recommendation contexts.
The heterogeneity in implementations and training procedures makes fair comparisons and reproducibility difficult.
Predictions from embedding models are notoriously hard to interpret without additional post-hoc techniques.

families.name: Rule-Based Reasoning and Mining
families.definition: Approaches that learn or apply first-order logical rules from knowledge graphs to predict missing facts and provide interpretable explanations.

properties.text: These methods extract weighted Horn rules or probabilistic logical rules to justify predictions.
Rule-based approaches like AnyBURL and SAFRAN offer fully interpretable alternatives to neural embedding models.
Techniques such as DRUM and RLvLR use differentiable or representation-learning-based methods to scale rule mining to large knowledge graphs.
Reinforcement learning can guide the generation and evaluation of rules to improve efficiency and effectiveness.
Rules can be mined from frequent predicate cycles or semantic association patterns in RDF data.

limitations.text: Traditional rule learning techniques are often inefficient and struggle to scale to web-scale knowledge graphs.
Aggregating predictions from multiple rules can suffer from redundancies if not properly handled.
Some approaches require manual effort or domain knowledge to define patterns and rules.
Rule-based methods may be limited in their ability to handle previously unseen entities in inductive settings compared to some embedding methods.

families.name: Graph Neural Network Explainability
families.definition: Post-hoc techniques designed to interpret the predictions of Graph Neural Networks by identifying important subgraphs, nodes, or edges.

properties.text: Methods like GNNExplainer and GraphLIME identify crucial graph components and node features that contribute to a specific prediction.
Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and saliency maps can be adapted to provide pixel-wise or feature-wise explanations for GNNs.
Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM) explainers like PGM-Explainer generate explanations in the form of PGMs approximating the prediction.
Differentiable edge masking can be used to identify unnecessary edges in GNNs for NLP tasks.
Model-level explainers like XGNN provide high-level insights into how GNNs work generally, rather than just instance-specific explanations.

limitations.text: Explaining GNNs is challenging due to the complex nonlinear transformations made over iterations.
Local explanations are often painstakingly customized for each instance, lacking a global understanding of the model.
There is no consensus on the definition of 'attribution' or ground truth for evaluating the faithfulness of these explanations.
Most existing explainers assume data instances are independent and identically distributed, which excludes relational models like GNNs in some frameworks.

families.name: Neurosymbolic and Hybrid Approaches
families.definition: Frameworks that integrate symbolic knowledge representation and reasoning with deep learning to enhance interpretability and performance.

properties.text: These approaches use knowledge graphs as underlying frameworks to provide terminology for representing explanations of machine learning classifiers.
Neurosymbolic computing seeks to combine robust learning in neural networks with reasoning and explainability.
Methods like TensorLog compile logical queries into differentiable functions within deep learning infrastructure.
Hybrid models can distill structured knowledge from differentiable path-based models into embedding-based recommenders.
Causal Bayesian Networks and Knowledge Graphs can be combined for interactive and intelligent root cause analysis in manufacturing.

limitations.text: Integrating knowledge graphs into deep learning models presents challenges in maintaining comprehensibility.
Purely data-driven methods like Causal Bayesian Networks have problems scaling to large-scale processes due to vast cause-effect relationships.
There is a need for well-founded knowledge representation to be effectively integrated with deep learning for sound explainability.

families.name: Explainable Recommendation Systems
families.definition: Techniques that generate recommendations along with intuitive explanations to improve user trust and transparency.

properties.text: These systems use knowledge graphs to provide traceable reasoning paths for the recommendation process.
Methods like LOGER and PGPR use neural logic reasoning or policy-guided path reasoning to generate faithful explanations.
Explanations can be generated by distilling structured knowledge or by initializing latent factors with semantic features from knowledge graphs.
Some approaches present both reasons for and reasons against a recommendation to enhance overall trust.
Tree-enhanced embedding models can provide concrete reasons for recommendations by exploring side information.

limitations.text: Prior research rarely considers the faithfulness of derived explanations to justify the decision-making process.
Current explanation techniques often strongly uphold recommended products rather than presenting balanced reasons.
Embedding-based recommendation models lack intrinsic explainability and suffer from data sparsity.

families.name: General Post-Hoc Explanation Methods
families.definition: Model-agnostic techniques that approximate the behavior of black-box models with interpretable surrogates to explain individual predictions.

properties.text: Methods like LIME and SHAP (implied by 'Unified Approach') explain predictions by learning interpretable models in the local vicinity of the prediction.
These methods are applicable to a wide range of classifiers, including deep learning models.
They help users understand the reasons behind predictions to assess trust and transform untrustworthy models.
Feature attribution methods compute the importance of each input feature to the prediction.

limitations.text: There is no consensus on the definition of 'attribution', leading to competing methods with little systematic evaluation.
These methods often assume data instances are independent and identically distributed, which may not hold for relational data.
Explaining black-box models for high-stakes decisions is argued to be less effective than using inherently interpretable models.
Visual explanations may not be expressive enough to grasp critical information relying on relations between sub-concepts.
Lack of consensus on the definition of 'attribution' and ground truth for evaluating feature importance methods.
Scalability of purely data-driven causal methods to large-scale, real-world processes with vast cause-effect relationships.
Need for unified treatment and taxonomy of GNN explainability methods.
Challenge of providing global understanding of GNN models rather than just instance-specific local explanations.
Ensuring the faithfulness of explanations generated by recommender systems and knowledge graph reasoning models.
Integration of knowledge graphs into deep learning models to create more comprehensible AI systems.
Addressing the sparse reward problem and bias towards spurious paths in reinforcement learning-based knowledge graph reasoning.
Developing methods that are both accurate and inherently interpretable for high-stakes decision-making domains.
